transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2028-05-14
Time: 15:30 - 16:32 UTC
Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Ethan Cole (Redwood AE), Maya Lin (Redwood SE), Carlos Reyes (Redwood CSM), Olivia Hart (Lyricom VP Product), James Park (Lyricom MLOps), Nina Gupta (Lyricom Finance)

Summary: Quick Q2 checkpoint to reconcile usage and spending, walk through a reliability incident from last month, and align on the canary/pilot plan for the next release.

[00:00] Ethan Cole: Hey everyone, thanks for making time today. Quick check, audio ok?
[00:05] Olivia Hart: Yep, good here.
[00:07] James Park: good.
[01:12] Ethan Cole: Cool. I'll kick off with a 2-minute top-line on what we saw in April — then Maya will dig into the spike and the proposed bench plan. Carlos will cover the contract and audit bits and then we'll close with next steps.
[02:05] Maya Lin: So for April, Lyricom's token volume spiked about 3.8x on two midweek days, primarily on the summarization route, looks like a combination of a marketing push and a reindex job that retriggered. There was prefix cache churn because the requests had variable prompts, so batching was less effective.
[02:48] James Park: yeah that reindex job should have been throttled, our fault. We didn't realize it hit the summarization endpoint rather than offline processing — we mis-flagged the env var.
[03:20] Olivia Hart: The finance team saw the line item jump and we want to understand what parts we can control and what are platform-level levers.
[03:42] Nina Gupta: Right, we got the invoice and it was sizable. We need to see scenario planning: if we run the new recommenders at 2x traffic, what does burn look like?
[04:10] Ethan Cole: Totally. On that, we've prepared a model that slices costs by route and by model family. There are clear levers: Dedicated capacity for steady baseline, burst via hosted, and smarter batching/prefix caching. We'll share the spreadsheet after the call.
[04:47] Maya Lin: Important note — for Lyricom's workload with long contexts, quantization helps CPU/GPU memory but affects latency slightly. The runtime supports 4-bit variants that reduce per-token cost; we should test quality delta on your eval set.
[05:30] James Park: Would that change our SLA? If we pick a quantized variant for production, what happens on fallbacks?
[05:44] Maya Lin: Fallbacks are policy-driven — typically we route to full precision if latency SLO allows, or we failover to a cheaper model for non-critical routes. You can set route-level policies in Console.
[06:10] Olivia Hart: On reliability — last month's incident, can we walk through what happened?
[06:22] Carlos Reyes: I'll summarize: on 2028-04-12 around 03:00 UTC, a regional capacity pressure caused queued requests which surpassed the autoscale headroom. A routing fallback kicked in but a small percentage of in-flight requests experienced timeouts for ~7-8 minutes while capacity rebalanced. We had an automated retry knob but it wasn't enabled for that route.
[06:58] James Park: we found the timeouts in our logs too; the SDK retried twice and then bubbled the 5xx up.
[07:20] Maya Lin: The mitigation we've proposed: increase buffer headroom for that route, enable kernel-level backpressure, and turn on automated retries with jitter in the SDK. Also add circuit-breakers on client side to avoid repeated hot retries.
[08:05] Olivia Hart: Can you quantify user-visible impact? How many requests failed?
[08:18] Carlos Reyes: Roughly 0.3% of production tokens were affected during the window equating to ~120k tokens. The cost impact was limited but customer-facing latency blips were noticed on a small set of sessions.
[08:45] Nina Gupta: That helps. From a billing perspective we need to understand both peak and sustained cost to evaluate reserved capacity vs hosted credits.
[09:10] Ethan Cole: For reserved/dedicated, you get predictable unit costs and latency SLOs — but you commit to monthly baseline. Hosted is elastic but has higher per-token marginal cost during bursts. We can model mixed modes: reserve baseline for 70% and allow hosted bursts for 30%.
[09:48] James Park: If we do 70/30 reserved/hosted, what about cold-start latency when bursts spin up?
[09:58] Maya Lin: We have warm pool options and burst capacity that pre-warms nodes; there's a tradeoff on cost. Also prefix caching reduces cold-start impact if sessions reuse prompts.
[10:20] Olivia Hart: Can you show us an example of the dashboard we'd get?
[10:25] Maya Lin: I'll pull up the Console — (screen-share noise) — here's the token breakdown per route, per-model. You can see the summary route is 58% of total tokens but accounts for 72% of latency-sensitive SLA hits.
[11:02] Ethan Cole: Note the per-token cost line — the recommender model is 1.8x the summarizer due to longer contexts and attention cost.
[11:27] Nina Gupta: Is there any quick wins to reduce spend today without degrading quality?
[11:34] Maya Lin: Yes: 1) aggressive prefix deduplication, 2) reduce max tokens on some routes, 3) soft-rate-limit background jobs, 4) eval quantized candidate for non-critical routes. Small config changes can cut 10-18% on the high-volume route.
[12:05] James Park: We can triage the background jobs first - I'll take ownership for that.
[12:12] James Park: (continues) Also on the instrumentation side, our telemetry for token counts is off by about 4% compared to Console, so we need to reconcile.
[12:28] Carlos Reyes: We'll export raw ingest logs and compare — Maya cc'd — to align counting.
[13:05] Olivia Hart: On roadmap alignment, we have a Q3 push for personalization and that increases real-time inference needs. We want to lock in a pilot cadence and SLA for canary rollouts.
[13:34] Maya Lin: For canary, recommended approach: A/B two small subsets (1% then 5%), monitor latency, error rate, quality regressions (we can plug your eval suite into our quality monitors), then escalate to 25% if stable. We also provide automatic rollback after quality regression thresholds.
[14:05] James Park: How do we measure quality regressions? BLEU/Rouge isn't perfect for recommendations.
[14:16] Maya Lin: Agreed — use your heuristic metrics plus golden prompt sets. We support custom eval hooks and divergence alerts tied to prompt sets; we'll show the config.
[14:40] Olivia Hart: On security and procurement, Nina has a checklist. Nina, any asks?
[14:49] Nina Gupta: Yes, we need SOC2 Type II evidence, KMS integration options, and audit log retention SLA to satisfy internal compliance. Also need SSO/SAML setup notes for our contractors.
[15:10] Carlos Reyes: We're SOC2 compliant and can share the report. For KMS, we support CMEK via major cloud KMS or customer HSM for Private deployments. Audit logs retention can be extended via add-on. We'll attach the docs.
[15:36] Olivia Hart: Great. Back to cost modelling: can you run two scenarios: conservative 50% reserved, 50% hosted; and aggressive 80% reserved?
[15:46] Ethan Cole: Yep, we'll send both. Expect the spreadsheet with per-route breakout and amortized model switching costs.
[16:02] James Park: For the bench, what metrics should we capture?
[16:10] Maya Lin: We'll capture p50/p90/p99 for tail latency, token/sec throughput, cost per 1M tokens, memory pressure, and failure rate under sustained QPS. Also KV cache hit ratio and batching efficiency.
[16:34] Olivia Hart: Sounds good. Can you also check what the cost delta is if we force 4-bit quantization vs full precision for the recommender?
[16:42] Maya Lin: Yes, we'll run the quantize-vs-fp sweep against your eval set. Expect a preliminary quality vs cost curve in the bench results.
[17:05] James Park: Our internal runbook needs a short checklist for on-call — what to change first during a spike. Can you provide a starter runbook?
[17:12] Carlos Reyes: We'll share a runbook template: increase burst headroom, enable retries with jitter, flip circuit-breaker thresholds, and escalate to Redwood SRE.
[17:40] Olivia Hart: Are there any platform-level changes planned that might affect our Q3?
[17:49] Maya Lin: We're launching an optimized kernel path for long-context models in June that should reduce p99 by ~15% for sequences >8k tokens. We'll flag it on your account and coordinate testing.
[18:10] Nina Gupta: That could justify higher baseline reserved capacity if latency improves.
[18:20] Ethan Cole: Good catch. We'll include that in the cost scenarios as a sensitivity.
[18:35] Olivia Hart: Any compliance gotchas for Private deployment vs Hosted?
[18:44] Carlos Reyes: Private gives you full control over network and keys, recommended for regulated PII workflows. Hosted can be configured with strict tenancy and KMS but some customers prefer Private for auditability.
[19:05] James Park: For our pilot, I'd prefer hosted burst with a dedicated baseline — simpler to start. If compliance needs grow, we can phase to Private.
[19:18] Maya Lin: That's a common path and minimizes ops lift initially.
[19:40] Ethan Cole: Ok to recap next steps: Ethan to send cost model, Maya to run bench and invite James, Carlos to send compliance docs. Anything else?
[19:52] Olivia Hart: Add the runbook and a recommended canary schedule.
[20:00] Nina Gupta: Please include the procurement timeline and what docs we need to sign off.
[20:12] Ethan Cole: Will do.
[20:18] (brief cross-talk, background noises)
[21:00] Olivia Hart: Quick question from James — in the model switching cost, do you include the rolling warm-up token overhead?
[21:10] Maya Lin: Yes we account for warm-up tokens and potential doubled traffic during migration windows; it's in the model under "migration overhead."
[21:38] James Park: ok great.
[22:00] Ethan Cole: Anything blocking the bench run scheduling?
[22:05] James Park: No, we'll free a staging cluster.
[22:12] Carlos Reyes: We'll draft the test plan and include CSVs for the token-level mapping.
[22:40] Olivia Hart: Great. If nothing else, let's recap in bullet and finish.
[22:55] Ethan Cole: Recap: 1) Redwood sends two cost scenarios + migration sensitivity, 2) Redwood runs 72-hour load bench and shares dashboard, 3) Redwood provides runbook and SOC2/KMS/audit docs, 4) Lyricom will throttle background jobs and prep staging for bench. Deadlines as noted earlier.
[23:30] Nina Gupta: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[23:40] Olivia Hart: Thanks all.
[23:45] (meeting ends)
